151	36\. I believe this adequate protection package is appropriate and consistent with market practice for priming DIP facilities in Chapter 11 cases. The adequate protection provided to Hollcroft Ventures and the Pre-Petition First Lien Secured Parties is designed to protect them against any diminution in the value of their collateral resulting from the Debtors\' use of cash collateral and the granting of the DIP liens.
152	
153	**E. Professional Fee Carve-Out**
154	
155	37\. The DIP Credit Agreement provides for a professional fee carve-out (the \"Carve-Out\") in the total amount of \$1,750,000, allocated as follows: (a) \$1,500,000 for fees and expenses of professionals retained by the Debtors; and (b) \$250,000 for fees and expenses of professionals retained by any official committee of unsecured creditors appointed in these cases (the \"Committee\"). The Carve-Out is triggered upon the occurrence of an Event of Default (as defined in the DIP Credit Agreement) followed by the delivery of a written notice by the DIP Lender to the Debtors (the \"Carve-Out Trigger Notice\"). I believe the Carve-Out is adequate and sufficient to ensure that estate professionals and Committee professionals can fulfill their fiduciary duties in these Chapter 11 cases.
156	
157	**F. Budget and Financial Reporting**
158	
159	38\. The Debtors\' postpetition operations and expenditures shall be governed by the 13-week DIP Budget, a copy of which is attached as Exhibit B to the DIP Credit Agreement. The DIP Budget sets forth the Debtors\' projected cash receipts and disbursements on a weekly basis for the initial 13-week period following the Petition Date. As noted above, the DIP Budget projects total receipts of approximately \$52.8 million and total disbursements of approximately \$56.4 million, including approximately \$3.2 million in restructuring professional fees.
160	
161	39\. Compliance with the DIP Budget shall be tested on a bi-weekly basis, with permitted variances of plus or minus 10% on total receipts and total disbursements, measured on a rolling two-week basis. The Debtors shall deliver to the DIP Lender bi-weekly budget variance reports, together with such additional financial information as the DIP Lender may reasonably request. I believe these reporting requirements represent appropriate controls that will provide transparency and accountability with respect to the Debtors\' postpetition financial performance.
162	
163	**G. Milestones.**
164	
165	40\. The DIP Credit Agreement includes the following case milestones (the \"Milestones\"), which are designed to ensure that the Debtors\' restructuring proceeds expeditiously and that estate value is preserved for the benefit of all stakeholders:
166	
167	> \(a\) **Entry of Interim DIP Order:** No later than 5 days after the Petition Date (March 19, 2025).
168	>
169	> \(b\) **Entry of Final DIP Order:** No later than 35 days after the Petition Date (April 18, 2025).
170	>
171	> \(c\) **Filing of Section 363 Sale Motion or Plan of Reorganization:** No later than 75 days after the Petition Date (May 28, 2025).
172	>
173	> \(d\) **Court Approval of Sale or Plan Solicitation Procedures:** No later than 110 days after the Petition Date (July 2, 2025).
174	>
175	> \(e\) **Closing of Section 363 Sale or Confirmation of Plan:** No later than 180 days after the Petition Date (September 10, 2025).
176	
177	41\. The DIP facility has a maturity date of December 14, 2025, which is nine months following the Petition Date (the \"DIP Maturity Date\"), or such earlier date as may result from the occurrence of an Event of Default, the effective date of a confirmed plan of reorganization, or the closing of a sale of substantially all of the Debtors\' assets under Section 363 of the Bankruptcy Code. In my view, the Milestones and DIP Maturity Date provide a reasonable and achievable framework for the Debtors to pursue a value-maximizing restructuring transaction.
178	
179	**H. Events of Default**
180	
181	42\. The DIP Credit Agreement contains customary events of default for a facility of this nature (each, an \"Event of Default\"), including, without limitation, failure to comply with the Milestones, budget variances in excess of the permitted thresholds, conversion or dismissal of the Chapter 11 cases, appointment of a trustee or examiner with expanded powers, a material adverse change in the Debtors\' business or financial condition, and failure to make any payment when due under the DIP Credit Agreement. In total, the DIP Credit Agreement enumerates approximately 28 events of default, each of which is more fully described in Article VIII of the DIP Credit Agreement. I believe the events of default are appropriately tailored to protect the DIP Lender\'s interests while affording the Debtors reasonable operational flexibility to pursue their restructuring objectives.
182	
183	**I. Credit-Bidding and Sale Process Rights**
184	
185	43\. Pursuant to the DIP Credit Agreement, Ironclad is granted an irrevocable right to credit-bid the full amount of its DIP claims --- up to the full \$55 million DIP Commitment amount, plus accrued and unpaid interest, fees, and expenses --- as well as its outstanding pre-petition second-lien claims, in connection with any sale of the Debtors\' assets under Section 363 of the Bankruptcy Code or any plan-related auction process. These credit-bidding rights are consistent with Section 363(k) of the Bankruptcy Code and provide important protections for Ironclad as both DIP Lender and a significant creditor of the estates.
186	
187	44\. In addition, Section 8.05 of the DIP Credit Agreement provides that Ironclad shall be designated as the stalking horse bidder in any Section 363 sale of the Debtors\' assets, subject to the entry of a sale procedures order by the Court. As stalking horse bidder, Ironclad will be entitled to a break-up fee equal to 3.5% of the proposed purchase price and expense reimbursement of up to \$2.0 million, payable in the event that a higher or better bid is selected. I believe these provisions serve an important function in the Debtors\' restructuring by providing a floor bid that ensures the estate will receive a minimum

ts outstanding pre-petition second-lien claims, in connection with any sale of the Debtors\' assets under Section 363 of the Bankruptcy Code or any plan-related auction process. These credit-bidding rights are consistent with Section 363(k) of the Bankruptcy Code and provide important protections for Ironclad as both DIP Lender and a significant creditor of the estates.

44\. In addition, Section 8.05 of the DIP Credit Agreement provides that Ironclad shall be designated as the stalking horse bidder in any Section 363 sale of the Debtors\' assets, subject to the entry of a sale procedures order by the Court. As stalking horse bidder, Ironclad will be entitled to a break-up fee equal to 3.5% of the proposed purchase price and expense reimbursement of up to \$2.0 million, payable in the event that a higher or better bid is selected. I believe these provisions serve an important function in the Debtors\' restructuring by providing a floor bid that ensures the estate will receive a minimum recovery and by incentivizing Ironclad\'s continued participation and investment in the Debtors\' restructuring process. The availability of a committed stalking horse bid benefits all stakeholders by providing certainty and establishing a baseline for any competitive auction.

**J. Releases, Waivers, and Lender Stipulations**

45\. Section 9.15 of the DIP Credit Agreement contains a stipulation (the \"Lender Stipulation\") pursuant to which the Debtors and their estates acknowledge and stipulate to the validity, priority, enforceability, and amount of Ironclad\'s pre-petition second-lien claims in the full amount of \$95 million outstanding under the Pre-Petition Second Lien Credit Agreement. This stipulation reflects the undisputed nature of Ironclad\'s pre-petition claims, which have been documented through a fully executed credit agreement and related loan documents, and is a customary condition in DIP facilities provided by pre-petition lenders.

46\. The proposed DIP orders provide that any official committee of unsecured creditors appointed in these cases shall have 30 calendar days from the date of its formation to investigate the DIP Lender\'s pre-petition claims and liens and, if appropriate, to commence a challenge proceeding with respect thereto. The expected timeline for Committee formation, based on discussions with the Office of the United States Trustee, is approximately 21 days following the Petition Date, or approximately April 4, 2025. The Final DIP Order hearing is currently scheduled for April 18, 2025. I believe that the 30-day investigation period provides the Committee with a reasonable and sufficient opportunity to evaluate the pre-petition claims and liens.

**[VI. The DIP Facility Satisfies the Requirements of Section 364 of the Bankruptcy Code]{.underline}**

47\. Based on my experience in structuring and providing DIP financing and my familiarity with the facts and circumstances of these Chapter 11 cases, I believe the DIP facility satisfies the requirements of Section 364 of the Bankruptcy Code.

48\. First, I am informed by the Debtors and their advisors that the Debtors were unable to obtain unsecured credit allowable as an administrative expense under Sections 364(a) or 364(b) of the Bankruptcy Code. Given the Debtors\' financial condition, the nature and extent of their pre-petition indebtedness, and the operational challenges they face, no lender was willing to extend postpetition credit on an unsecured or administrative-expense-only basis. The grant of first-priority priming liens and superpriority administrative expense claims was necessary to induce Ironclad to extend credit to the Debtors and is authorized under Sections 364(c) and 364(d) of the Bankruptcy Code.

49\. Second, I believe the terms of the DIP facility, including the interest rate, fees, and other costs, are fair and reasonable and represent the best available terms for the Debtors under the circumstances. The pricing reflects the risks inherent in providing credit to a debtor in possession, the Debtors\' financial condition and credit profile, and the competitive dynamics of the market for DIP financing to mid-market industrial borrowers. The Debtor was unable to secure financing on an unsecured basis or on terms more favorable than those offered by Ironclad, as confirmed by the thorough marketing process conducted by Stonebridge Partners LLC, as described in Section IV above. After evaluating all available alternatives, the Debtor determined that Ironclad\'s proposal offered the most favorable combination of pricing, structure, certainty of execution, and speed to closing.

50\. Third, the DIP liens and superpriority administrative expense claims are necessary to induce Ironclad to extend credit. Ironclad would not have agreed to provide the DIP facility without the lien and priority package described above, which is consistent with standard market protections in DIP financing transactions.

51\. Fourth, the Debtor exercised sound business judgment in selecting Ironclad as the DIP Lender and in entering into the DIP Credit Agreement on the terms described herein. The Debtors\' decision was informed by the advice of experienced legal and financial professionals, a review of the available alternatives, and a consideration of the Debtors\' immediate and projected liquidity needs. The roll-up component of the DIP facility was a necessary condition to securing Ironclad\'s commitment and represents fair value in light of the new money being made available to the estate. I believe the DIP facility, taken as a whole, provides the Debtors with the liquidity and financial stability necessary to pursue a value-maximizing restructuring for the benefit of all stakeholders.

52\. For all of the foregoing reasons, I respectfully submit that the DIP facility satisfies the requirements of Section 364 of the Bankruptcy Code and that approval of the DIP Motion is in the best interests of the Debtors, their estates, and their creditors.

**[VII. Conclusion and Prayer for Relief]{.underline}**

53\. For the reasons set forth above, I respectfully request that this Court grant the DIP Motion and enter the proposed Interim DIP Order and, following a final hearing, the proposed Final DIP Order, which orders would, among other things:

> \(a\) authorize the Debtors to enter into and borrow under the DIP Credit Agreement on the terms and conditions set forth therein;
>
> \(b\) grant the DIP liens and DIP Superpriority Claims as set forth in the DIP Credit Agreement and the proposed Interim DIP Order;
>
> \(c\) authorize the Debtors\' use of cash collateral;
>
> \(d\) approve the adequate protection package for Hollcroft Ventures National Bank, N.A. and the Pre-Petition First Lien Secured Parties as set forth herein and in the proposed Interim DIP Order; and
>
> \(e\) schedule a final hearing on the DIP Motion for a date no later than April 18, 2025.

54\. The DIP financing is essential to the Debtors\' continued operations and the preservation of going-concern value for all stakeholders, including creditors, employees, customers, vendors, and the communities in which the Debtors operate. Without the DIP facility, the Debtors will be unable to fund their operations and will face the immediate and irreversible destruction of enterprise value.

55\. I am available to testify and answer questions at the interim hearing on the DIP Motion, currently scheduled for March 19, 2025, and at the final hearing, and I am prepared to provide such further testimony or information as the Court may require.

I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the United States of America that the foregoing is true and correct to the best of my knowledge, information, and belief.

Dated: March 17, 2025 Stamford, Connecticut

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Marcus Holt Managing Partner Ironclad Capital Partners, LLC 200 Harbor Point, Suite 1400 Stamford, CT 06902

**EXHIBIT LIST**

The following exhibits are referenced in this declaration and are attached to or filed in connection with the DIP Motion and the DIP Credit Agreement. Capitalized terms used herein and not otherwise defined have the meanings ascribed to them in the DIP Credit Agreement.

**Exhibit A** --- Senior Secured Superpriority Debtor-in-Possession Credit Agreement, dated as of March 14, 2025, by and among Redstone Manufacturing Holdings, Inc. and its debtor affiliates, as borrowers, and Ironclad Capital Partners, LLC, as DIP Agent and DIP Lender (with all schedules and exhibits thereto).

**Exhibit B** --- 13-Week DIP Budget (attached as Exhibit B to the DIP Credit Agreement).

**Exhibit C** --- Pre-Petition Second Lien Credit Agreement, dated as of June 15, 2021, by and among Redstone Manufacturing Holdings, Inc. and its affiliates, as borrowers, and Ironclad Capital Partners, LLC, as administrative agent and collateral agent (excerpts).

S=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/sbx.sh; R=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/vendor/harvey-labs/results/bankruptcy-restructuring/identify-issues-in-dip-credit-agreement/claude-code-session/20261016-040700; $S $R 'mkdir -p /workspace/build && cat > /workspace/build/content1.py <<'"'"'PYEOF'"'"'
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
HEADER = [
 ("TO:", "Supervising Partner"),
 ("FROM:", "Restructuring Associate"),
 ("RE:", "In re Redstone Manufacturing Holdings, Inc., Case No. 25-10347 (JKW) (Bankr. D. Del.) - Issues in the Senior Secured Superpriority DIP Credit Agreement with Ironclad Capital Partners, LLC"),
 ("CONTEXT:", "Prepared ahead of the Final Hearing set for April 18, 2025 (objection deadline April 11, 2025, per Interim Order para. 26)"),
 ("PRIVILEGED:", "Attorney work product - prepared in anticipation of litigation"),
]

SCOPE = [
 "You asked me to review the DIP Credit Agreement dated as of March 14, 2025 (the \"DIP Agreement\" or \"CA\") among Redstone Manufacturing Holdings, Inc. (\"Redstone\" or the \"Borrower\"), the Subsidiary Guarantors, and Ironclad Capital Partners, LLC (\"Ironclad\"), as DIP Lender and DIP Agent, and to flag provisions that are problematic, off-market, or inconsistent with each other or with the rest of the case record. I reviewed the full text of each of the following: (1) the DIP Agreement, with its exhibits and schedules; (2) the Ironclad Term Sheet dated March 10, 2025 (\"TS\"); (3) the Interim DIP Order entered March 19, 2025 (\"IO\"); (4) the Declaration of Marcus Holt dated March 17, 2025 (\"Holt Decl.\"); (5) the excerpts from the Pre-Petition Second Lien Term Loan Credit Agreement (\"2L CA\"); and (6) the 13-week DIP Budget workbook (Summary, Detail, and Assumptions tabs) (\"Budget\").",
 "This memorandum is written from the estate's perspective, meaning the issues the Debtor's fiduciaries must resolve and the objections we should expect from the U.S. Trustee, an official committee (the \"Committee\"), Hollcroft Ventures National Bank, N.A. (\"Hollcroft\"), and the seven non-Ironclad second-lien lenders. Unless I say otherwise, section references are to the DIP Agreement. Severity ratings work as follows. High: a provision likely to block approval, expose the estate to material value loss, or create a legal defect. Medium: off-market, or a likely objection we should negotiate. Low: a drafting or conforming point. My statements about \"market\" practice reflect general experience with middle-market Delaware DIP facilities. Statutory and rule references should be cite-checked, including against the current text of Del. Bankr. L.R. 4001-2, before anything is filed.",
]

EXEC_SUMMARY_INTRO = "The DIP Agreement is drafted heavily in the lender's favor, and in several places it is internally inconsistent. Ironclad is not a neutral third-party lender. It is the 66% holder of, and the agent under, the second-lien debt. It uses the facility to (i) lift $35 million of its own junior debt ahead of the $93.3 million first lien and ahead of its fellow second-lien lenders, (ii) obtain stipulations and releases that bind the estate on a timetable that ends before any investigation can be completed, and (iii) take control of the sale process. On new money alone the economics are severe. The issues that most need attention are:"

EXEC_POINTS = [
 ("Debtor-entity mismatch (High).", "The DIP Agreement (Recital A) and the Interim Order treat Redstone as the only debtor, and say the three subsidiaries have not filed. Yet the subsidiaries grant \"first-priority priming\" liens under Section 364(d) (Sections 2.07 and 11.04; IO para. 5(a)(i)). The Holt Declaration says all four entities filed and are jointly administered. Either way, the documents are defective. If the subsidiaries did not file, the Court has no Section 364 power over their assets, and they cannot prime Hollcroft's or the second lien's liens on those assets without consent. If they did file, they are not parties to the Interim Order, and the Superpriority Claims run only against Redstone's estate. The Budget shows that 100% of operating receipts are collected by the subsidiaries."),
 ("Roll-up (High).", "$35 million of Ironclad's own second-lien debt (and none of the other holders' debt) becomes priming, first-priority DIP debt senior to Hollcroft's first lien (Section 2.02). That is 1.75x the $20 million new-money commitment, and 8.75x the $4.0 million of new money the Budget actually projects drawing in the first 13 weeks. $5 million rolls on an interim basis. The roll-up appears to breach the 2L CA's pro rata and sacred-rights provisions (Sections 2.11, 9.03(d), 11.02(b)(v), (vii), (d)) and its payment subordination to the first lien (2L CA Sections 9.01, 9.03(a), (c))."),
 ("Non-Ironclad second-lien lenders primed with no adequate protection (High).", "Section 5.04(b) is \"Reserved.\" The 2L CA's consent to priming applies only if all second-lien lenders receive adequate protection pro rata (2L CA Sections 9.05(c), 9.06). Section 364(d)(1)(B) is not satisfied as to the $32.3 million held by the seven other lenders."),
 ("Stipulations, releases and challenge period (High).", "The Committee gets 30 days from its appointment (the TS said 60 days), no other party has standing, and the DIP Agreement provides $0 for investigation (the IO allows $25,000). The Final Order, due April 18, must embed the stipulation as Court findings (Section 3.02(b)). That is before the Investigation Period even expires, about May 4, 2025, on the Holt Declaration's own projected April 4 Committee formation date. Section 9.15(b) also releases unknown claims, including equitable subordination under Section 510, in favor of Ironclad and its affiliates."),
 ("Economics (High/Medium).", "The Upfront Fee (3.00%) and Exit Fee (2.50%) are charged on the full $55 million, including the roll-up. Together they total $3,025,000, which is 15.1% of the new-money commitment; $1,925,000 of that is attributable to the roll-up alone. The Exit Fee is owed on any termination, including conversion, dismissal or a refinancing. The Agent Fee is $600,000 a year, paid in advance to a sole lender that is also the agent. Default interest is +400 bps and compounds. The rolled-up debt is repriced from the 2L CA's SOFR+575 bps with a 1.00% floor to SOFR+850 bps with a 3.50% floor."),
 ("Lender professional fees (High).", "Lender professional fees are uncapped and paid within 10 Business Days. They are expressly free of any review by the U.S. Trustee, the Committee or the Court, and are payable \"without regard to ... any order of the Bankruptcy Court\" (Sections 2.09(c), 5.03, 9.03(a)). They cover Ironclad's defense of its pre-petition second-lien position, and the estate also indemnifies Ironclad for the Chapter 11 Case generally (Section 9.03(b))."),
 ("Carve-Out (High/Medium).", "Under the DIP Agreement, the pre-trigger Carve-Out is capped by the Approved Budget. The Interim Order makes it uncapped. The Budget's single $3.2 million professional-fee line mixes in the uncapped lender fees. The Committee receives only $250,000 against the Debtor's $1.5 million. There is no Chapter 7 trustee carve-out and no investigation budget."),
 ("Sale process control (High).", "Ironclad must be designated stalking horse, with a 3.5% break-up fee plus up to $2 million of expense reimbursement (Section 8.05). It may credit bid up to $82.7 million plus interest and fees, including $27.7 million of un-rolled second-lien debt that is junior to the first lien (Section 8.04). The Borrower must \"actively oppose\" any limit on the credit bid, and the Court's refusal to approve credit-bid rights is itself an Event of Default (Section 7.01(s))."),
 ("Defaults and remedies (High/Medium).", "Several defaults are hair-triggers. Three examples: a cross-default that pre-petition defaults already trip (Section 7.01(u)); a \"sole discretion\" MAE that includes \"prospects\" and has no carve-out for the Chapter 11 filing, which makes the Section 4.04(b) representation untrue when made; and defaults triggered merely by third parties filing motions (Section 7.01(i), (j), (aa)). The variance test is two-sided with no cure period. The Borrower may not even talk to alternative lenders (Section 6.07(c)). Ironclad holds a veto over estate professionals (Section 6.08). The remedies standstill is narrower than the Interim Order's."),
 ("Budget arithmetic errors (High).", "The weekly disbursements sum to $57.4 million, not the $56.4 million stated in the DIP Agreement, the Interim Order and the Holt Declaration. The true 13-week burn is therefore $4.6 million, not $3.6 million. Week 1 \"Net Cash Flow After Financing\" is overstated by $1.3 million. Correctly computed, ending cash is about $2.6 million, not $3.9 million. All variance testing runs against this flawed budget."),
 ("Wrong-document and identity errors (Medium).", "The DIP Agreement misdates the Pre-Petition Second Lien Credit Agreement (October 15, 2020, versus the actual June 15, 2021) and the First Lien Credit Agreement (June 22, 2018, versus March 22, 2019 per the 2L CA). It conflicts with the Interim Order on its own date (March 14 versus March 19) and its parties. Facility locations and EINs conflict across the documents. These errors go directly to the stipulations, the collateral descriptions and the mortgages."),
]
PYEOF
echo done'

  i=["Pre-trigger fees.      "Trigger mechanics. Under the CA definition, the Carve-Out Trigger Notice goes to the Borrower, its counsel and the Committee, but not the U.S. Trustee (the IO adds the U.S. Trustee).      "Diligence flags. The record contains no perfection diligence (UCC searches, mortgages, deposit account control agreements) for the second lien. Commercial tort claims are second-lien collateral only if “identified from time to time” (2L CA § 1.01). The DIP Agreement misdescribes the second-lien agreement’s date (Part A). These are the kinds of issues a challenge would explore."],
  r="Limit the stipulation to the validity, priority and amount of the second-lien claims as of the Petition Date, in an amount that is fixed and reconciled to the Register and accrued interest.   i=["Under § 9.15(c), only “the Committee” may investigate, and only for 30 calendar days from its appointment. No other party in interest has standing.   i=["The Borrower must designate Ironclad “or an affiliate or designee” as stalking horse in any § 363 sale of substantially all assets.   r="Delete § 8.05, or make stalking-horse selection subject to the Debtor’s business judgment and a market test, with any bid protections to be sought by separate motion under O’Brien.  dict(t="Credit-bid rights are overstated and insulated from the Court", s="High",
  p="§§ 8.04(a)–(c), 7.01(s); TS § 11; Holt Decl. ¶ 43; 2L CA §§ 9.01, 9.03(b)",
  i=["Section 8.04(b) sets Ironclad’s credit bid at up to $55 million of DIP Obligations, “representing the full DIP Commitment,” plus $27.7 million of un-rolled second-lien debt, for up to $82.7 million plus interest, fees and expenses. Undrawn commitment cannot be bid; on the Budget, only $4 million of new money is drawn in 13 weeks. Second, the $27.7 million of un-rolled second-lien debt is junior to Hollcroft’s first lien (2L CA §§ 9.01, 9.03(b)). Del. 2014)). Rolled-up and second-lien claims that are subject to a pending challenge are classic candidates.",
     "Section 8.04(c) requires the Borrower to “actively oppose” any limit on credit bidding. Section 7.01(s) makes it an Event of Default if the Court fails to approve the credit-bid rights or limits them in any order. That converts the Court’s exercise of its § 363(k) discretion into a default, and it conflicts with the Debtor’s fiduciary duty to maximize value."],
  r="Limit the credit bid to allowed DIP Obligations actually outstanding. Make any credit bid of second-lien debt subject to cash payment of senior claims, and make credit bidding of roll-up or second-lien debt subject to the challenge period. Expressly preserve the Court’s “for cause” authority. Delete the “actively oppose” covenant and § 7.01(s)."),
]))

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
SECTIONS = []
SECTIONS.append(("I. Covenants, Events of Default, and Remedies", [
 dict(t="Covenants that restrict the Debtor’s fiduciary duties", s="High",
  p="§§ 6.07(a)–(c), 6.08, 3.01(i), 8.01, 8.04(c), 7.01(q); TS § 18 (Exclusivity)",
  i=["Section 6.07(c) bars the Debtor from even engaging “in discussions or negotiations with any party regarding any alternative or replacement post-petition financing” without Ironclad’s sole-discretion consent. The TS exclusivity clause, by contrast, expired on the earlier of execution or April 1, 2025. Section 6.07(c) has no fiduciary out and no end date, and it blocks the market test that would show whether these terms are the best available. Combined with the Exit Fee, it locks in the facility. Section 6.08 requires Ironclad’s approval of every estate professional, which intrudes on the Debtor’s statutory retention rights under § 327 and the Court’s authority. Section 3.01(i) made Ironclad-approved retentions a condition of closing."],
  r="Delete § 6.07(c), or add a fiduciary out permitting discussions of a refinancing that pays the DIP in full in cash. Delete § 6.08. Limit § 6.07(a)–(b) to non-consensual priming financings that do not pay the DIP Obligations in full."),
 dict(t="Events of Default that are hair-triggers, triggered by third parties, or already tripped", s="High",
  p="§§ 7.01(d), (e), (g), (i), (j), (k), (m), (p), (r), (s), (t), (u), (x), (aa), (bb); definition of “Material Adverse Effect”; § 4.04(b); TS § 10; 2L CA § 7.01(h); IO ¶¶ 7(b), 12",
  i=["Cross-default (§ 7.01(u)). This is triggered by “a default or event of default under any material indebtedness … (other than the DIP Obligations)” above $250,000. The First Lien and Second Lien facilities are in default by reason of the filing itself (for example, 2L CA § 7.01(h)), so read literally the DIP is in default at closing. Section 6.01(b)–(c) expressly permits that pre-petition debt to remain outstanding.",
     "MAE (§§ 7.01(m), (bb); definition; § 4.04(b)). The MAE is determined “in the sole discretion of the DIP Lender,” extends to “prospects,” and has no carve-out for the commencement of the case or the events that customarily follow from it. Section 4.04(b) represents that no MAE has occurred since the FY2024 financial statements, and that representation is brought down at each borrowing (§ 3.03(b)). The Chapter 11 filing itself makes that problematic. Clauses (m) and (bb) duplicate each other. The 2L CA MAE, by contrast, is objective.",
     "Third-party and Court-action triggers. Defaults are triggered by: the filing by any party of a motion to convert or dismiss (§ 7.01(i)); the filing by any party of a motion for a trustee or examiner (§ 7.01(j)); stay relief granted to any creditor on assets over $500,000 (§ 7.01(k)); termination of exclusivity by the Court (§ 7.01(p)); any post-period challenge by any party (§ 7.01(r)); the Court’s refusal to approve credit-bid rights (§ 7.01(s)); and the filing of any § 506(c) motion by any party (§ 7.01(aa)). Defaults keyed to someone else’s filing give Ironclad leverage over creditors and over the Court’s own processes. Market practice limits these to motions filed or supported by the Debtor, or to entry of an order.",
     "Budget variance (§ 7.01(g); definition of “Permitted Variance”). Variance is tested at “plus or minus” 10% on both receipts and disbursements, so favorable performance, such as higher collections or lower spending, is also a default. There is no cure period. IO ¶ 7(b) tests only unfavorable variance (disbursements over 110%, receipts under 90%) and gives a 3-business-day cure after notice. The Budget Assumptions describe a 5-business-day cure and 3-business-day reporting, while § 5.01(c) requires reporting within 5 Business Days.
